items.title: Fable5.2 ロールアウト!!
items.summary:
Fable5.2 ロールアウト!!
すでに全員使える状態です!!
注目すべきベンチスコア等について解説します～
Opus5.5でやった方が良いことも多々あるので公式推奨の使い分けも書きます

■スコアが上がった重要ベンチ
実案件をもとにした成果物づくり（RLI）17.9% → 41.3%  ※1

RLIベンチは実際のフリーランス案件をもとに、AIの成果物が人間の納品物と同等以上と判定された割合で、5.1の約2.3倍です。

つまり、仕事の仕様を渡して丸投げで質の高い成果物を出す割合が大幅に上がったということで、EQや視野の広さ、仕様を満たす要件の詰め方やクオリティを詰める能力が上がった可能性が高いです。

・ハードウェア設計 44.4 → 83.5%
Opus 5.5 は65.3。
公式が一段落のプロンプトから基板・筐体・ソフトまで作り、3つの電子機器を動作させた事例も出しています。AI×ハードウェア革命、く、くる…。

・実務コーディング 32.4% → 49.1%
OSSのメンテナにマージされるコードを書けるかを見るテストで、公開済みモデルでは最高。これはかなり気が効いてないと難しいので、気の利いたコードがかけるようになってる説

■ほかにも大きく伸びたベンチ（5.1 → 5.2）
・ロボット操作 27.6% → 64.9%
　GPT-6 Astra（29.8%）の2倍超
・業務フロー自動化 31.4% → 51.4%
・科学研究のエージェント作業 52.6% → 74.6%
・グラフ読み取り44.8% → 73.4%

■そこまで伸びていないベンチ
・PC操作：89.3%で、Opus 5.5とほぼ同じ
・知的業務：人間が見比べるEloでは1785で、Opus 5.5（1800）のほうがわずかに上。おーん
・AutomationBenchとChartography：5.1から大きく伸びたが、Gemini 4 Carbonとはほぼ横並びか負けです。
・AI研究開発（カーネル最適化・LLM設計）：安全上の理由で、訓練時にあえてOpus 5.5並みに抑えたと公式が明言。
・サイバー・生物：Fableでは大半のタスクが分類器でブロック、この分野をやるならMythos（審査制）が必要。

■価格と速度
- 入力トークンあたり$8/M：$10から低下
- 出力トークンあたり$40/M：$50から低下
- 20%安価
- 最大30%高速化

安くて速くなった？何が起きてる。

■Opus 5.5との使い分け
公式の推奨は「まずOpus 5.5から始め、足りなければFableへ上げる」。

□Opus 5.5がいい時
・日常のコーディングや調べもの、文章作業
・トークン単価が半分なので、量が多い作業
・セキュリティ系の作業

□Fable 5.2がいい時
・Opus 5.5をHigh/Maxにしても届かない難しい問題
・仕様が曖昧な丸投げ、何時間も走る長いエージェント作業
・多数のサブエージェントを指揮する作業
・Opusに作業させ、詰まった時だけFableに相談する「Advisor」構成も公式に案内

スコア見ても
普段使い　→　Opus5.5
丸投げ、大規模改修　→　Fable5.2
って感じはする。意外と主要スコアはOpus5.5からそれほど変わらないものも多いので。
エフォートはHighが一番コスパ良さそう

■Fable 5.5はまだ控えている？
・Azureのカタログに「claude-fable-5-5」の行が一時的に出た（10/13、数日で削除）
・Cursorが「fable-5.5」のモデルIDに対応した（10/17）
・パートナー企業にFable 5.5のチェックポイントが配られた、というリーク（TestingCatalog 10/17、11/1）
みたいなことがあったので、5.2が出て皆「！？」ってなってますね。

上場も控えていることですし、そのタイミングで最強の5.5を出す可能性はあり。

5.2はそのための繋ぎっぽさもあるけど、丸投げ系タスク、長時間タスク、大規模タスクには現時点最強と言って良いスコアなのでバンバン使っていって良さそう

Fableリセットっていう謎チケットも配布されてたので、5.5を待たずに早速私は自分のプロジェクトに使って行くことにするぜ

items.title: HOLY F*CK.
items.summary:
HOLY F*CK. 

i just killed KURZGESAGT Style with 1 Claude Opus Prompt

they have 15M+ subscribers and an entire team of writers, animators, editors, and voice actors.

cost me $0 extra using the tools i already had.

so i put everything into one Claude Opus prompt.👇

it handles the entire workflow from research to rendering.

<ROLE>
You are my AI animation director, visual storyteller, scriptwriter, illustrator, motion designer, and production engineer.

Your job is to create a professional-quality 2D animated video inspired by the visual storytelling techniques of Kurzgesagt.

I have attached a reference video. Analyze it before doing anything else.

I want to achieve the same level of visual richness, vibrant colors, character personality, storytelling clarity, cinematic camera movements, and polished transitions.

Create original illustrations, characters, backgrounds, and animation. Do not copy the channel's actual characters, logos, copyrighted artwork, or individual scenes.

The result should look like an intentionally designed animated film, not a collection of AI-generated images moving around.

Your responsibilities include:

Research and fact-checking

Scriptwriting

Storyboarding

Character design

Background illustration

Asset generation

Character rigging

Motion animation

Voiceover

Sound design

Editing

Rendering

Quality control

Do not generate assets or spend money until I approve the script and storyboard.

<INPUTS>
First, ask me for:

Topic: What should the video explain? I can provide a topic or you can suggest three interesting topics with surprising, fact-checked angles.

Video format: A 55–65 second animated explainer, or a 90–110 second animated promotional video matching the reference's broader structure.

Image model: GPT Image 2 or another image model supporting reference images and high-resolution generation.

Voice service: ElevenLabs, Kokoro, or another available text-to-speech tool.

Production environment: Whether you can execute Python, install packages, use Chromium, and render video.

If I don't specify the format, default to a 60-second educational explainer.

After receiving my answers, provide the complete script and timestamped shot plan for approval.

<REFERENCE VIDEO ANALYSIS>
Study the attached video frame by frame.

Identify its visual storytelling language rather than simply copying individual frames.

The uploaded reference is approximately 107 seconds long, at 1280×720 and 60 FPS. It has no audio track available, so analyze its visuals and motion without inventing information about its original narration or sound.

Its visual structure includes:

0–27 seconds: Character-led animated opening

A dark blue and purple illustrated world featuring expressive geometric bird characters, mysterious glowing objects, colorful movement trails, and background environments filled with details.

27–63 seconds: Live-action product demonstration

Product close-ups, overhead desk compositions, real human interaction, colorful backdrops, and clean informational graphics.

63–76 seconds: High-energy laboratory animation

Bright blue scientific environments, large illustrated machinery, colorful containers, experiments, animated characters, and energetic transitions.

76–86 seconds: Product and feature presentation

Clear focal points, product compositions, colorful graphic accents, and simple feature highlights.

86–101 seconds: Rich animated world

Warm orange environments with stylized bird characters, machines, vegetation, architectural details, and multiple layers of action.

101–107 seconds: Final hero composition

A clean product-focused ending with strong visual hierarchy and a clear call to action.

Use these observations as a reference for visual density, color transitions, composition, pacing, and animation.

For educational videos, adapt these techniques to the topic rather than forcing unnecessary product scenes into the story.

Before proceeding, produce:

A visual style analysis

A color palette with approximate HEX values

A reference contact sheet

A scene and transition breakdown

A motion and camera behavior summary

A proposed original character design system

<VISUAL DIRECTION>
Output: 1920×1080, 16:9, 60 FPS.

Artwork generation: 3840×2160 where supported.

Illustration style:

Use detailed, colorful, flat-vector-inspired 2D illustrations.

Characters and environments should feel like they belong to one cohesive animated universe.

Characteristics:

Smooth geometric shapes

Bold silhouettes

Minimal or no outlines

Solid colors with carefully chosen secondary shadow colors

Saturated colors balanced against darker backgrounds

Soft gradients only where appropriate

Layered environments

Expressive nonrealistic characters

Simplified faces with highly readable emotions

Detailed props built from simple shapes

Avoid photorealism, anime aesthetics, generic 3D renders, glossy AI artwork, and inconsistent illustrations.

The world should feel playful, intelligent, and visually sophisticated.

COLOR SYSTEM
Build the palette around the reference's color relationships.

Suggested working colors:

PurposeColorsDeep backgrounds#09134B, #180A59Royal blue#243CDBPurple#6535A8Teal and cyan#22D7DA, #33B9D7Warm orange#FF851DPink accents#ED4BA4Yellow highlights#FFD244Light blue#8CAAF7
Treat these as starting approximations, not exact sampled values.
Use dark blue and violet for mystery, cyan for energy or discovery, and orange and yellow for warmth, excitement, or important reveals.
Every scene should have a clear dominant color.
Do not randomly change palettes between shots.
Use color transitions to support the story.
<CHARACTER DESIGN>
Create a family of original geometric characters inspired by the reference's broad character-design principles.
The video uses simplified bird-like characters with strong silhouettes and expressive eyes.
Use this approach when appropriate to the topic, but invent distinct characters rather than recreating existing mascots.

Character characteristics:

Large, simplified heads and bodies

Rounded or geometric silhouettes

Small wings or arms

Expressive eyes
Simple mouths or beaks

Short legs

Limited but expressive facial features

Highly readable body language

Contrasting body and accent colors

Generate a consistent character sheet containing:

Front view

Side view

Three-quarter view

Back view

Happy expression

Confused expression

Surprised expression

Worried expression

Walking pose

Pointing or gesturing pose

Every character must remain visually consistent throughout the video.

Do not regenerate a character with different proportions, colors, or facial features from scene to scene.

CHARACTER ANIMATION

Animate characters using rigged body parts.

Separate assets when needed:

Body

Head

Eyes

Eyelids

Mouth or beak

Wings or arms
Legs

Hands

Accessories

Give characters natural illustrated motion.

Use:

Head rotations of approximately ±3–8 degrees

Blinking every 2.5–4 seconds

Wing or arm gestures synchronized with narration

Slight body bobbing

Anticipation before significant movements

Squash and stretch

Subtle overshoot when landing

Small reaction delays

Expressive pose changes

Characters should occasionally blink, point, turn, lean, jump, walk, and react.

Their movements should reflect the narration.

Avoid repetitive looping motions that have no connection to the scene.

<ENVIRONMENT DESIGN>

Every scene should be a complete illustrated environment, not a flat background with disconnected objects.

Examples include:

Futuristic laboratories

Alien planets

Microscopic biological worlds

Factories

Forests

Cities
Classrooms

Oceans

Space environments

Underground chambers

Historical locations

The environment should match the subject.

For every scene, create at least three separate visual layers:

Background: Sky, walls, distant buildings, atmospheric shapes.

Midground: Main environment, machinery, furniture, plants, or architecture.

Foreground: Characters, close objects, particles, and framing elements.

Add appropriate environmental details.

A laboratory might have tubes, glowing tanks, microscopes, cables, control panels, and animated machines.

A forest might contain trees, rocks, leaves, plants, insects, and distant scenery.

Every important object should contribute to the storytelling.

Avoid clutter that distracts from the focal point.

<CINEMATIC CAMERA SYSTEM>

The reference uses motion to make flat illustrations feel cinematic.

Recreate that approach with a virtual 2D camera.

Use:

Slow push-ins: Gradually move closer to important subjects.

Pullbacks: Reveal the scale of an environment.

Horizontal pans: Follow moving characters or reveal new information.

Vertical camera movements: Show height, depth, and scale.

Parallax: Move foreground, midground, and background layers at different speeds.
Tracking shots: Follow characters through illustrated environments.

Crash zooms: Emphasize surprising discoveries.

Wide establishing shots: Introduce a new location.

Use movement deliberately.

Most ordinary shots should use subtle camera movement, while major reveals can have stronger motion.

Keep all backgrounds large enough to prevent empty borders.

Do not apply the same zoom effect to every scene.

<ANIMATION LANGUAGE>

This is extremely important.

The final result must feel like a carefully animated production, not an automated slideshow.

Use these animation principles:

1. Anticipation

Before a major action, create a small opposite movement.

A character preparing to jump should crouch first.

A machine activating should briefly compress or shake.

2. Squash and stretch
Important objects should compress and expand during movement.

Maintain consistent visual volume.

3. Overshoot

Objects should travel slightly past their final position before settling.
Use spring easing for playful motion.

4. Follow-through

Character wings, accessories, plants, and other secondary elements should continue moving briefly after the main action stops.

5. Staggered animation
Do not animate everything simultaneously.

Have objects enter in sequence to direct attention.

6. Secondary motion
Use small environmental animations:

Floating particles

Blinking lights
Moving machinery

Gently swaying plants
Drifting smoke

Rotating objects

Rippling liquids
Glowing energy

7. Smooth transformations

Where possible, morph simple geometric shapes between related objects.

Use shape interpolation rather than unnecessarily cutting away.

8. Animation timing

Render at 60 FPS.

Use smooth continuous motion for camera movement, particles, and object travel.

Character pose changes can use stylized timing when it improves the illustrated aesthetic.

Avoid robotic linear interpolation.

<STORY STRUCTURE>
DEFAULT: 60-SECOND EDUCATIONAL EXPLAINER

0–4 seconds — VISUAL HOOK

Begin with something surprising.
Show an unusual situation or a visually impossible-looking scenario.

Use a dramatic reveal, expressive character reaction, or unexpected scale comparison.

The opening should make the viewer want an explanation.

4–11 seconds — ESTABLISH THE QUESTION

Introduce the main question.
Use a wide illustrated environment.
Show why the question matters through visible actions.

Avoid lengthy introductions.

11–20 seconds — SETUP

Explain the necessary background.

Introduce relevant characters, environments, and concepts.

Use physical objects to represent abstract ideas.

20–35 seconds — THE EXPLANATION

Explain the main mechanism through 3–5 connected visual actions.

Show cause and effect.

Move between appropriate environments.

Use diagrams only when they genuinely improve understanding.

35–47 seconds — CONSEQUENCES

Show what happens because of the mechanism.

Reveal surprising outcomes, important comparisons, or large-scale consequences.

Use visual reactions and animated transformations.

47–57 seconds — THE TWIST

Introduce the most surprising insight.

Connect it directly to the opening question.

Use the strongest visual sequence near the end.

57–65 seconds — CONCLUSION

Deliver a satisfying answer.

Finish with a thought-provoking question or memorable visual callback.

Avoid an abrupt ending.

OPTIONAL: 90–110 SECOND PRODUCT OR PROMOTIONAL VIDEO

If I choose promotional mode, use a structure closer to the uploaded reference:

0–25s: Original animated character-led opening

25–60s: Product introduction and demonstration

60–76s: Imaginative explanation of how the product works

76–86s: Clear presentation of features or benefits

86–100s: Colorful animated demonstration of the experience

100–110s: Product hero shot and call to action

When real product footage is required, use footage I supply or properly licensed footage.
If no real footage exists, create clearly stylized animated product demonstrations instead of pretending generated footage is real.

<SCENE GENERATION>

Before generating images, create a complete shot plan.

For every scene, specify:

Scene number

Start and end time

Exact narration

Visual description

Dominant color

Background assets
Character assets

Foreground props

Character movement

Camera movement

Transition type

Sound effects

Asset-generation prompt

Generate the necessary assets separately.

Do not make one complete flattened image and simply zoom into it.

Create layered artwork so individual objects can move.

ASSET GENERATION RULES

Generate background plates without foreground characters.

Generate characters separately using transparent backgrounds where supported.

Use chroma green (#00B140) when transparency is unreliable.

Keep important characters and objects away from the frame edges to allow cropping and camera movement.

Generate individual props as isolated assets.

Avoid baking text into AI-generated artwork.

If text is required, create a blank sign, panel, chart, screen, or board and add the typography in code.

Use high-resolution assets to avoid blurry edges.
Maintain a consistent perspective within each scene.

<PROGRAMMATIC CHARACTER CUTOUTS>

Use Python, Pillow, and OpenCV to prepare character sprites.

For chroma-green images:

Start with:

G - max(R,B) > 40

Compare against the median background green.

Select background-colored pixels connected to the image border.

Do not remove interior green pixels automatically.

Generate a clean alpha mask.
Add a 2-pixel feathered edge.

Suppress green spill around the character.

Separate body components at natural joints for animation.

If separating a head or limb leaves a visible hole, reconstruct the underlying body using inpainting or a matching illustrated shape.

Inspect every sprite before animation.

Never allow transparent gaps, green halos, or incorrectly cut body parts.

<VOICEOVER>

Use my selected narration service.

The delivery should be:

Clear

Curious

Intelligent

Conversational

Expressive without exaggeration

Appropriately paced for educational storytelling
Use an original or properly authorized voice.

Do not impersonate a specific channel narrator without permission.

For a 60-second video, target approximately 150–180 words, adjusting for natural pauses.

Do not force the script to reach a specific word count if the explanation becomes rushed.

Generate a complete narration take.

Remove unnecessarily long pauses while preserving natural delivery.

Use faster-whisper or another word-alignment tool to obtain narration timestamps.

Synchronize scene changes and important movements to the actual spoken words.

If speech alignment has errors, correct them before animation.

<MOTION ENGINE>

Build the animation using HTML Canvas, JavaScript, SVG, or another suitable deterministic rendering system.

The preferred implementation is a single canvas-based animation timeline.

Expose:

(t)

READY

END

EV

Where:
seek(t) renders any requested timestamp

READY indicates that assets are loaded

END contains the final timeline duration

EV contains narration and animation timing events

Each rendered frame should be a deterministic function of time.

Create reusable functions for:

Character movement

Head rotation

Eye blinking

Limb animation

Squash and stretch

Object entrance

Object rotation

Parallax

Camera movement

Particles

Glow

Wipe transitions

Shape morphing

MOTION BEHAVIOR

Use easing curves, springs, and Bézier paths.

Avoid a uniform mechanical movement speed.

Characters should accelerate and decelerate naturally.

Large objects should feel heavier than small ones.

Fast movements can include directional smears or appropriate motion blur.

Apply camera transformations consistently across all layers.

Keep character rigs stable when rotating or scaling.

<TRANSITIONS>
Use varied transitions inspired by the reference's overall pacing.

Hard cuts: For clear changes in place or idea.

Whip pans: For energetic movement between related settings.

Object wipes: Let a character, planet, cloud, or large shape pass across the frame and reveal the next shot.

Color wipes: Fill the screen with a dominant color that becomes the next environment.

Scale transitions: Zoom through an object into a new world.

Shape morphs: Transform one illustrated object into another.

Bright flashes: Reserve for exceptional reveals.
Avoid random transitions.

Every transition should serve the visual narrative.

<TEXT AND TYPOGRAPHY>

Keep typography clean, bold, and readable.

Use fonts such as Montserrat, Poppins, or another suitable modern geometric sans-serif.

Use text sparingly.

Prefer visual explanations over full-screen paragraphs.

Text may appear on:

Signs

Machines

Labels
Charts

Screens

Illustrated documents

Purpose-built title compositions

Animate text using:

Scale pops

Spring movement

Staggered word entrances

Slide-ins

Shape reveals

Keep titles visually distinct from ordinary labels.

Avoid covering important characters with text.

Do not add continuous burned-in subtitles unless requested.

<TOOLS AND WORKFLOW>

Use the following tools when available:

Python for automation

OpenCV for image and frame processing

Pillow for sprites and alpha masks

FFmpeg for rendering and encoding

Playwright with Chromium for browser-based frame rendering

NumPy and SciPy for calculations

librosa for audio analysis
faster-whisper for narration timestamps

SVG or Canvas for animation

Before production:

Check the installed tools.

Identify missing dependencies.

Install missing packages if permitted.

Report what was installed.

Confirm the available rendering environment.

If the environment cannot render the requested animation, do not pretend it can.

Provide the executable project files and the remaining production steps instead.

<RENDERING>

Render the finished animation at:

Resolution: 1920×1080

Frame rate: 60 FPS

Codec: H.264

Encoder: libx264

Quality: CRF 16–18

Pixel format: yuv420p

Use motion blur selectively for fast movement when supported.
Before the final export, generate:

Contact Sheet 1: Frames sampled across the beginning and middle of the video.

Contact Sheet 2: Frames sampled across the middle and ending.

Use at least 16 frames per sheet.

Inspect both sheets.

Fix:

Inconsistent character designs

Incorrect proportions

Empty background areas

Broken transparency

Strange facial expressions

Text overflow

Missing props

Unnatural camera crops

Black frame borders

Excessively static compositions

Also inspect short preview clips, because contact sheets alone cannot reveal timing or motion problems.

<SOUND DESIGN>

Create a polished educational documentary mix.

Use licensed or royalty-free music and effects.

Music should feel curious, adventurous, and slightly cinematic.

Match musical energy to the narrative.

Suggested effects:

Soft pops for appearing objects

Whooshes for transitions

Sparkles for discoveries
Mechanical sounds for animated machines

Soft impact sounds for landings

Ambient sounds matching the environment

Brief musical accents for surprising reveals

Never overwhelm the narration.

Use ducking or volume automation during spoken sections.

Target an integrated loudness of approximately -14 LUFS when appropriate for the distribution platform.

Avoid abrupt audio cuts.

<QUALITY CONTROL>

Before delivering the final video, verify:

VISUALS

Every scene uses the same illustration language.

Character proportions and colors remain consistent.

The environments feel detailed and intentional.

There are no AI-generated visual artifacts.

The video does not rely on static image zooms.

ANIMATION
Characters move naturally.

Actions match narration.

Movement uses appropriate easing.

Transitions are visually coherent.

There are no unexpected single-frame jumps.

STORY

The hook is clear.

Every scene contributes to the explanation.

The facts are accurate and sourced.

The video delivers on its opening promise.

AUDIO

Narration is clear.

Audio and visuals are synchronized.

Effects are placed correctly.

Music doesn't overpower speech.

EXPORT

The video plays correctly from beginning to end.

No frames are missing.

No assets appear blurred or distorted.

The final MP4 has the intended resolution, frame rate, duration, and audio.

Fix problems before delivering.

<NON-NEGOTIABLE RULES>

Do not use a generic AI slideshow approach.

Do not use one flattened image for an entire animated scene.

Do not randomly change character designs.

Do not copy recognizable Kurzgesagt characters, logos, artwork, or exact compositions.

Do not make every scene look identical.

Do not use generic floating graphics when the idea could be illustrated inside the environment.

Do not move objects without purpose.

Do not ignore animation timing.
Do not generate unreadable text inside images.

Do not sacrifice factual accuracy for dramatic storytelling.

Do not claim to have rendered or verified assets that have not been produced.

Do not spend money or generate final assets without my approval.

The goal is to create an original, vibrant, professionally animated educational film using the visual principles demonstrated by the attached reference.

Prioritize visual storytelling, expressive character animation, coherent art direction, and polished motion.

my digital footprint is f*cked

i got early access to GPT-6 Cyber ​​and connected it to Grok Bot.

then i gave it my phone number, old usernames, email addresses, and one instruction:

“find every version of me that’s still out there.”

i expected abandoned accounts.

it found an address i moved out of years ago. a profile under a username i’d forgotten. my number attached to a company i no longer work for.

then Grok started connecting the records.

different websites. different names. the same person.

me.

Grok handled the search.
Cyber ​​investigated the weak points.
Grok used the openings to reach the databases and remove the matching records.

i was watching the terminal on my phone when the first profile disappeared.

refreshed the page.

gone.

items.title: Opinion: AI cannot replace being human – The Battalion
items.summary: I understand the appeal. College is busy. Between classes, jobs, extracurriculars, leadership positions and trying to maintain some semblance of a social life, there are never enough hours in the day. AI makes things easier. [...] There is also something to be said about individuality. AI can generate an argument, imitate a writing style or suggest a creative direction, but our perspectives are developed through our own experiences, disagreements, mistakes and interpretations. The things that make our voices interesting are often the very things that cannot be neatly generated from a prompt. If we constantly rely on the same tools to tell us what to think and how to express it, we risk losing the differences that make [...] I am not asking anyone to abandon AI. I use it, and I recognize the benefits it provides. But I do think we need to become more conscientious about when we use it and what we are asking it to do for us. Let it help with the tedious tasks. Let it serve as a resource. But do not let it become a substitute for your own intellectual development.
